title: Block 1.1 — Place Value & Rounding

blocks.title: Place Value & Reading Large Numbers
teacherCues: After this block, ask: "Why do we group digits in threes?"
Display a large place-value chart on the board and call on students to read numbers aloud.

discoveryHook.scenario: The world population is about 8,100,000,000. If you see that number without commas, you might misread it. How do we make sense of such huge numbers? We use a place‑value chart that groups digits in threes — the same system that turns eight billion one hundred million into 8,100,000,000.

deepThink.prompt: Why do we group digits in threes from the right when writing large numbers? What would happen if we didn't use commas or a pattern?
deepThink.placeholder: Think about how you would read 1000000000 without any separators…

explanation: A [[def:whole number|a counting number from 0, 1, 2, …]] can be written using the [[kw:decimal system]], a place‑value system based on powers of 10. The position of a digit tells you its value.

To read a numeric number aloud, separate it into groups of three digits, starting from the right, using commas. Each group has a name: units, thousands, millions, billions, trillions. Within each group, there are ones, tens, and hundreds.

Read each three‑digit group as if it were alone, then add the group name (except 'units'). [[imp:Do not use the word "and".]] Hyphenate numbers from twenty‑one to ninety‑nine. Zero is a placeholder — you don't read it, but it keeps other digits in the right place.
[[note:Show the class a place‑value chart on the board and point to each group as you read the number.]]

graphData.title: Place-value chart
graphData.alt: Chart showing ones, thousands, millions, billions, trillions

formulaCard.title: Steps to read a whole number
formulaCard.formula: Read each group of three digits and add the group name.
notes: 1. Insert commas every 3 digits from the right.
2. Read each group as a 3‑digit number.
3. Add the group name (except for units).

examples.title: Example A — thousands
steps: Read the units: nine hundred forty‑eight.
Combine: Seven thousand, nine hundred forty‑eight.

examples.title: Example B — thousands and units
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner why you say 'forty‑eight thousand' and not 'forty eight thousand'.
steps: Whole: Forty‑eight thousand, seven hundred seventy‑five.

examples.title: Example C — billions
steps: Answer: Eight hundred fourteen billion, four hundred ten million, three hundred thirty‑five thousand, four hundred fourteen.

brainDump.prompt: Without looking: list the group names from units up to trillions in order. Then write the rule about using 'and'.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: [[imp:Do NOT say 'seven thousand and nine hundred forty‑eight'.]] The word 'and' is reserved for the decimal point. Also, remember the hyphen in 'forty‑eight' — it makes reading clearer.

hints: Group into thousands (12) and units (506).
Read the thousands, then the units. No 'and'.
The millions group is 3; thousands is 090; units is 020. Remember: don't read the zeros.
Zero in the hundreds place of thousands group — just say 'ninety thousand'.
Millions group: 40 → forty million. Thousands group: all zeros → skip. Units: 007 → seven.
No 'and', no mention of the missing thousands.

challengeCorner.prompt: The national debt is about 31,400,000,000,000. Write this number in words.
hints: First, find the group names: the leftmost group is trillions (31), then billions (400).
Write the trillions group in words, then the billions group.

blocks.title: Writing Numeric Numbers from Verbal Form
teacherCues: Cold-call: "What's the most common mistake when writing numbers from words?"
Emphasize the need for leading zeros in groups like "five hundred two thousand".

discoveryHook.scenario: A news headline says: 'Company profits reached three hundred twenty‑five million dollars.' To enter that into a spreadsheet, you need to write 325,000,000. Knowing how to convert words to digits is a key business skill.

deepThink.prompt: Why is it so important to keep track of the place value of each digit when writing a number from words? What happens if you forget a zero in a group like 'five hundred two thousand'?
deepThink.placeholder: Think about the value of each group name…

explanation: To convert a verbal number to numeric form, use a [[kw:place‑value chart]] to position each digit correctly. Each group name (thousand, million, etc.) tells you where to place the digits.

Work from left to right. Write the digits of each named group, then add zeros to fill the remaining places in that group so it has three digits. Remember to insert commas every three digits from the right.
[[imp:If a group has fewer than three digits, you must add zeros to the left to make three digits — except for the leftmost group.]]
[[note:Practice by having students write numbers in a blank place‑value chart.]]

formulaCard.title: Verbal to numeric steps
formulaCard.formula: Convert each group to three digits and combine.
notes: 2. Write digits in each group, left to right.
4. Insert commas every 3 digits from the right.

examples.title: Example A — millions and thousands
examples.prompt: Write 'five million, one hundred eighty‑one thousand' in numeric form.
steps: Millions group: 5 → write 5 (no leading zeros needed for leftmost group).
Thousands group: one hundred eighty‑one → write 181.
Units group: not mentioned → fill with 000.

examples.title: Example B — missing hundreds in thousands
examples.prompt: Write 'five hundred two thousand' in numeric form.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner why you need a zero in the hundreds place of the thousands group.
steps: Thousands group: five hundred two → 502 (the zero is in the hundreds place).

examples.title: Example C — millions and thousands
examples.prompt: Write 'twenty‑two million, five hundred fifty‑six thousand' in numeric form.

brainDump.prompt: Without looking: write the steps for converting a verbal number to digits. Then write an example with 'thirty million, four thousand'.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: [[imp:When a group like 'five hundred two thousand' is written, many students forget the zero and write 52,000 instead of 502,000.]] The zero in the hundreds place is essential to keep the digits in the correct place.

questions.prompt: Write 'seven thousand, nine hundred forty‑eight' in numeric form.
hints: Thousands: 7; units: 948.
After writing the thousands, add a comma and then write the units as a three-digit number.

questions.prompt: Write 'forty‑eight thousand, seven hundred seventy‑five' in numeric form.
hints: Thousands group: 48; units group: 775.
Combine the thousands group and units group with a comma, keeping three digits in each.

questions.prompt: Write 'three hundred million, two hundred thousand, fifty' in numeric form.
hints: Millions: 300; thousands: 200; units: 050.
Don't forget the zero in the tens place of the units group.

challengeCorner.prompt: Write 'four billion, sixty‑two million, eight hundred thousand, nine' as a number.
hints: Billions: 4; millions: 062; thousands: 800; units: 009.
Make sure each inner group has exactly three digits, using leading zeros if needed.

blocks.title: Converting Parts of a Million, Billion, etc., to Whole Numbers

discoveryHook.scenario: Ford Motor is investing \$3.5 billion to build a battery plant. You see numbers like \$2.7 million in business reports. How do you convert these 'decimal parts' of a large unit into a regular whole number you can enter in a calculator?

deepThink.prompt: Why do companies use decimals like \$3.5 billion instead of writing all the zeros? What advantage does this shorthand have?

explanation: Numbers like \$3.5 billion are a mix of a decimal and a word name. To convert, drop the decimal point and insert a comma, then add zeros so that the leftmost digit ends in the word name of the amount (million, billion, etc.).
[[imp:You must add enough zeros so that the number actually is in the billions or millions — otherwise the value changes.]]
[[note:This is a practical skill for reading financial news.]]

formulaCard.title: Conversion steps
formulaCard.formula: Multiply by the unit value (1,000,000 for million, etc.).
notes: 1. Drop the decimal point and insert a comma.
2. Add zeros so the leftmost digit ends in the word name (million, billion, etc.).

examples.title: Example A — billions
examples.prompt: Convert \$3.5 billion to a whole number.
steps: Multiplying by 1,000,000,000 moves the decimal point 9 places right: 3.5 → 3,500,000,000.

examples.title: Example B — millions with one decimal
examples.prompt: Convert \$2.7 million to a whole number.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner why the number becomes 2,700,000, not 27,000.

examples.title: Example C — hundredths of a billion
examples.prompt: Convert \$0.75 billion to a whole number.
steps: Moving the decimal 9 places right gives 750,000,000.

brainDump.prompt: Without looking: write the steps to convert \$4.2 trillion to a whole number.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: [[imp:Students often miscount zeros. If you have \$3.5 million, that is \$3,500,000 — not \$35,000 or \$350,000.]] Always check by multiplying: 3.5 × 1,000,000.

questions.prompt: Convert \$5.2 million to a whole number.
hints: Drop the decimal point; place 5 in the millions place.
5.2 million = 5.2 × 1,000,000. Multiply to find the result.

questions.prompt: Convert \$0.48 billion to a whole number.
hints: Think: moving the decimal 9 places to the right. What number do you get?

questions.prompt: Convert \$12.6 trillion to a whole number.
hints: Write the 12, then convert .6 trillion to billions, and add all zeros.

challengeCorner.prompt: A company's profit was \$3.05 billion. Write this as a regular whole number.
hints: Move the decimal 9 places to the right and insert commas.

blocks.title: Rounding Whole Numbers to a Specific Place
teacherCues: Check for understanding: "What happens if the digit to the right is exactly 5?"
Use a number line to visually show why 9,362 is closer to 9,400 than 9,300.

discoveryHook.scenario: A concert reports attendance of 23,487. News headlines might say 'about 23,500 attended'. Rounding makes numbers easier to understand and remember. It's a daily business tool.

deepThink.prompt: Why is it useful to round numbers? In what situations would it be misleading to use an exact number?
deepThink.placeholder: Think about budgets, populations, or sports statistics…

explanation: [[def:rounding|replacing a number with an approximate value that has fewer significant digits]] is a three‑step process: identify the place value to keep, look at the digit to its right, round up if it's 5 or more (or keep if less), then change all digits to the right to zeros.
Rounding does not change the size of the number drastically; it just simplifies it. The rounded number is often an estimate.
[[imp:When rounding, the identified digit may increase, but digits to its left never change.]]
[[note:Use a number line to show why 9,362 rounds to 9,400 and not 9,300.]]

formulaCard.title: Rounding steps
formulaCard.formula: Look at the next digit; if 5 or more, round up.

legend.meaning: decide to round up or not

notes: 1. Underline the digit in the place you want to round.
2. Look at the digit to the right. If ≥5, add 1 to the underlined digit. If <5, keep it.
3. Change all digits to the right of that place to zeros.

examples.title: Example A — to nearest hundred
steps: Digit to the right is 6 (≥5) → round up the 3 to 4.
Change all digits to the right to zeros: 9,400.

examples.title: Example B — to nearest thousand
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner why the thousands digit 7 becomes 8, not 6.
steps: Next digit is 9 (≥5) → round up the 7 to 8.

examples.title: Example C — to nearest ten
steps: Tens place is 4. Next digit is 5 (≥5) → round up 4 to 5.

brainDump.prompt: Without looking: write the three rounding steps and apply them to round 4,326 to the nearest hundred.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: [[imp:Many students forget to change the trailing digits to zeros.]] For 9,362 to nearest hundred, the correct rounded number is 9,400, but sometimes they write only 9,4 and stop. Always write the full number with zeros.

hints: The tens digit is 9, next digit is 2 (<5).
So the tens digit stays the same, and the ones digit becomes zero.
Hundreds digit is 3, next digit is 4 (<5) → keep 3.
After keeping the hundreds digit, change the tens and ones to zeros.
Thousands digit is 4, next digit is 7 (≥5) → round up to 5.
Then change all digits to the right to zeros, leaving a multiple of a thousand.

challengeCorner.prompt: Round 1,598,342 to the nearest ten thousand.
hints: Ten‑thousands place is 9 (second digit from left: 1,598,342).
The digit to the right is 8 (≥5) — adjust the ten‑thousands and carry if needed, then zero out the rest.

blocks.title: Rounding All the Way & Word Problems
teacherCues: Ask: "Why would a manager want numbers rounded all the way?"
Walk through the Tootsie Roll example together before students try the Kellogg problem.

discoveryHook.scenario: The average cost to raise a child to age 18 is about \$310,000. Rounded 'all the way', it becomes \$300,000 — quick, easy, and still useful for planning. Rounding all the way means rounding to the first digit, leaving only one nonzero digit.

deepThink.prompt: What does 'rounding all the way' mean? Why would you ever want to round a number to only one nonzero digit?

explanation: Rounding all the way is simply rounding to the leftmost digit. After rounding, only that digit remains nonzero; all others become zeros.
Use the same rounding steps: identify the leftmost digit, look at the digit to its right, round up if ≥5, then change all other digits to zeros.
[[imp:This method gives the roughest approximation, but it's great for quick estimates and checking reasonableness of answers.]]
In word problems, use the Blueprint Aid: list Facts, what you're Solving for, Steps to take, and Key Points. Then convert verbal numbers to numeric before rounding.

formulaCard.title: Rounding all the way
formulaCard.formula: Keep only the first digit nonzero; all others zero.
notes: 2. If the next digit ≥5, add 1 to the leftmost digit.
3. Change all other digits to zeros.

examples.title: Example A — simple rounding all the way
steps: Leftmost digit is 7. Next digit is 8 (≥5) → round 7 up to 8.

examples.title: Example B — millions
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner why the first digit 1 becomes 2.
steps: Leftmost digit is 1 (hundred‑millions). Next digit is 9 (≥5) → 1 becomes 2.
Change all other digits to zeros: \$200,000,000.

examples.title: Example C — profit word problem
examples.prompt: Tootsie Roll's profit was twenty‑two million, five hundred fifty‑six thousand dollars. Round this profit all the way.
steps: Leftmost digit is 2 (ten‑millions). Next digit is 2 (<5) → keep 2.

brainDump.prompt: Without looking: explain 'round all the way' and round \$5,181,000 all the way.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: [[imp:Students sometimes round each digit individually — that's wrong. Only one digit remains nonzero.]] Also, always convert verbal numbers to numeric before rounding.

hints: Leftmost digit is 6, next digit is 3 (<5) → stays 6.
Then all other digits zero, giving a number with three zeros at the end.
Leftmost digit 4, next 7 (≥5) → 5.
After adjusting the leftmost digit, zero out all places to the right.

questions.prompt: Kellogg's sales were five million, one hundred eighty‑one thousand dollars. Round this sales figure all the way.
hints: Convert to numeric: \$5,181,000. Leftmost digit 5, next 1 (<5) → keep 5.
After keeping the leftmost digit, turn all other digits to zeros.

challengeCorner.prompt: A company's profit was \$502,000. Round this profit all the way.
hints: Leftmost digit 5, next digit 0 (<5) → keep 5.
Change all digits after the first one to zeros.

presenterNotes: For the place value block, display a large place-value chart on the board and call on students to read numbers aloud.
When covering verbal-to-numeric, emphasize the need for leading zeros in groups like 'five hundred two thousand'.
In rounding, use a number line to visually show why 9,362 is closer to 9,400 than 9,300.
The rounding all the way block includes a word problem with the Blueprint Aid — walk through the Tootsie Roll example together before students try the Kellogg problem.
